title: Alphabet Sheds $766B in Worst Month as Valuation Drops to 2012 Low

tickers.name: Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. Class A Common Stock

summary:
Alphabet erased $766 billion in market value in October, its worst monthly loss on record, as a 12.6% post-earnings plunge on Oct. 29 pushed its price to earnings ratio to the lowest level since 2012. This week's selloff alone wiped out as much as $477 billion—more than SpaceX, Intel, Nvidia and Amazon lost combined and the steepest single day percentage drop since Alphabet's 2004 initial public offering—even as retail traders on Robinhood logged record one day net purchases of the stock.

The rout followed third quarter results where total revenue of $127.58 billion and earnings of $2.12 a share missed consensus estimates of $127.93 billion and $3.01. Search and Other revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion, falling short of the $64.85 billion forecast and dropping below 50% of total revenue for the first time even as query growth reached a five year high. Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said rapid growth in AI Mode queries weighed on results "because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI mode."

Capital expenditures jumped 114% from a year earlier to $51.36 billion, outrunning $42.3 billion in operating cash flow and leaving free cash flow at negative $9.1 billion for a second consecutive quarter, a reversal from a $24.6 billion quarterly surplus in the first quarter of 2025. Management kept its 2026 capital spending forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion and projected a further increase in 2027. Google Cloud revenue rose 103% to $30.71 billion and operating income tripled to $11.1 billion, though net income was dragged down by $8.2 billion in net other expenses tied to an unrealized loss on Alphabet's SpaceX stake.

selectedTweets.bestBit: Alphabet spent $9 billion more than it took in, its second negative quarter in a row, and this morning its stock fell 12%.
selectedTweets.text:
A year ago, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta generated $60.7 billion of free cash flow in a single quarter. This summer, $7.4 billion.

They didn't sell less. Revenue grew 19% at Microsoft, 25% at Alphabet and 26% at Meta. What changed is the bill: $125.6 billion in three months for data centers, chips and servers, double what they spent a year earlier. Meta put 54 cents of every dollar of revenue into capex. Alphabet spent $9 billion more than it took in, its second negative quarter in a row, and this morning its stock fell 12%. If it closes down more than 9.77%, it will be its worst day after earnings since going public in 2004.

The detail that worries me most is in Google's search numbers. Search ads grew 12% and still missed expectations. Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer, said part of the reason is that AI Mode makes less money per search. So Google is spending record sums to build a product that earns less than the one it replaces.

For twenty years these were the best businesses ever invented. You wrote the code once, sold it to billions of people, and almost every new dollar of revenue fell to the bottom line. AI doesn't work like that. Every answer runs on a chip someone had to buy and on electricity someone has to pay for. Big Tech is turning into something closer to a utility: huge upfront costs, long paybacks, and profits that depend on keeping the machines full.

That can still be a great business. But it is a different business, and investors are only starting to price it that way.

The old moat was code. The new one is cash.
